answer_text:
Assume the interval is nondegenerate, i.e. \(t_0<t_1\). We will show that the given condition forces \(f\) to be identically zero.

Suppose, for contradiction, that \(f\not\equiv 0\). Then there is some \(t_*\in I\) such that

\[
f(t_*)\neq 0.
\]

Since \(f\) is \(C^k\) and hence continuous, \(f\) has a constant sign in some small neighborhood of \(t_*\) and is bounded away from zero there. Therefore we can choose numbers

\[
t_0<a<b<t_1
\]

such that either

\[
f(t)\ge m>0 \quad \text{for all } t\in[a,b],
\]

or

\[
f(t)\le -m<0 \quad \text{for all } t\in[a,b]
\]

for some \(m>0\).

Now construct a smooth bump function supported in \([a,b]\). Define

\[
\phi(x)=
\begin{cases}
e^{-1/(1-x^2)}, & |x|<1,\\[4pt]
0, & |x|\ge 1.
\end{cases}
\]

This function is \(C^\infty\), nonnegative, and positive on \((-1,1)\). Set

\[
\eta(t)=\phi\!\left(\frac{2t-a-b}{b-a}\right).
\]

Then \(\eta\in C^\infty(\mathbb{R})\), \(\eta\ge 0\), \(\eta>0\) on \((a,b)\), and \(\eta=0\) outside \([a,b]\). In particular,

\[
\eta(t_0)=\eta(t_1)=0.
\]

Now define \(g\) by

\[
g(t)=
\begin{cases}
\eta(t), & \text{if } f(t)\ge m \text{ on }[a,b],\\[4pt]
-\eta(t), & \text{if } f(t)\le -m \text{ on }[a,b].
\end{cases}
\]

Then \(g\in C^\infty(I)\subset C^k(I)\) and \(g(t_0)=g(t_1)=0\). Moreover,

\[
f(t)g(t)\ge m\eta(t)\ge 0
\]

for all \(t\in[a,b]\), and the inequality is strict on \((a,b)\). Hence

\[
\int_{t_0}^{t_1} f(t)g(t)\,dt
=
\int_a^b f(t)g(t)\,dt
\ge
m\int_a^b \eta(t)\,dt
>0,
\]

which contradicts the hypothesis that the integral is zero for every such \(g\).

Therefore our assumption that \(f\not\equiv 0\) is false, so

\[
\boxed{\text{Yes, } f(t)\equiv 0.}
\]

If one allows the degenerate case \(t_0=t_1\), then the integral is automatically zero and the conclusion need not hold; the statement is true for the usual nondegenerate interval case \(t_0<t_1\).
